title: Cloudflare launches Search for Agents: one toggle lets AI agents search your site directly
summary: Site owners no longer need to build their own retrieval backend: turn on one toggle in the Cloudflare dashboard and your site is automatically indexed, exposing a search endpoint under your own domain that AI agents can discover on their own.
ai_summary: Cloudflare has launched Search for Agents, turning website search that previously had to be created and wired up manually into a single dashboard toggle. Once enabled, it automatically creates an AI Search instance for your domain, crawls and indexes your content, and injects metadata into every page so any AI agent can discover and call the /.well-known/search endpoint on your own domain. Results are returned as Markdown rather than as an answer generated by another model, so agents can use them directly as source material. It also natively supports the new HTTP QUERY method, which became RFC 10008 in June 2026. The feature is open to all users; the free plan works but has limits, and usage is billed under AI Search pricing. The biggest limitation is that Cloudflare has not published a specific quota for the free tier.
brief: Flip one toggle and it automatically creates an AI Search instance, then crawls and indexes your site.
Metadata is automatically injected into every page, so agents can discover the /.well-known/search endpoint themselves and reuse it.
It returns retrieved content in Markdown, not an AI-generated answer.
It natively supports the HTTP QUERY method from RFC 10008; the free plan is available with limits.

blocks.p: Cloudflare already had a service called AI Search: it indexes your content so you can add search to any application or agent without building a complete retrieval backend yourself. It has also supported using your website as a data source for a while, automatically crawling pages and converting them into an index.

The catch is that enabling AI Search for a website still meant doing the work yourself: you had to manually create and configure the instance, then do the integration work to place the search endpoint under your domain and make sure agents knew where to find the index and how to use it.

Search for Agents condenses all of that into one toggle. Turn it on for your zone in the dashboard, and Cloudflare automatically creates the AI Search instance, starts indexing your content, and makes search discoverable and callable from your own domain.

sections.h: What happens behind the scenes after you turn it on?

blocks.p: The toggle is under Quick Actions on the zone page in the dashboard, and you can also enable it via the API. Once enabled, Cloudflare automatically creates the AI Search instance and starts crawling and indexing the content in your zone; see the developer docs for details on how crawling works.

The instance is created with default settings, and you can enable reranking or adjust options like caching at any time. Because it is still an AI Search instance underneath, all the standard features are there: the public REST API, MCP endpoints, calling it from Workers, or embedding a search box for human visitors.

What can be searched, and who can search it, is still constrained by your domain's existing settings—such as bot management, AI Crawl Control (which controls which AI crawlers can access your site), and WAF rules.

sections.h: How do agents know your site can be searched?

blocks.p: An endpoint alone isn't enough—agents have to know it exists first. Search for Agents automatically advertises it on every page of your site.

For HTML responses, it injects a set of meta tags into the page's <head>: agent:instructions tells agents to use this search endpoint instead of crawling page by page, agent:endpoint gives the endpoint URL, agent:method specifies GET, and agent:documentation points to the docs.
If you also have Markdown for Agents enabled, an agent requesting the page with Accept: text/markdown receives the same information in YAML front matter.

sections.h: What comes back? How is it different from letting an AI answer directly?

blocks.p: Once an agent discovers the endpoint, it can call it directly. A plain GET request—for example, searching for "cloudflare artifacts"—returns relevant pages with their content converted to Markdown and ranked by relevance score. In the example, the first result scores 1.000 and the second 0.951.

Depending on your AI Search configuration, agents can also ask natural-language questions, such as "What is the maximum push size for Cloudflare Artifacts?", and the endpoint returns relevant document snippets.

The key difference is this: the endpoint returns retrieved content, not a generated answer. The agent already has its own model and conversation context; it needs the raw information from your site, not another model answering on its behalf.

fig.code:
curl "https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search?q=cloudflare+artifacts"

curl -X QUERY 'https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search' \
  --data 'What is the maximum payload size per ingestion request in Basin Pipelines?'

curl -X QUERY 'https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"q":"How many bulk import requests per minute does Email Service allow?"}'

sections.h: What is the new HTTP QUERY method?

blocks.p: In addition to plain GET, Search for Agents natively supports the new HTTP QUERY method. QUERY is an IETF Proposed Standard, published as RFC 10008 in June 2026, and Cloudflare's James Snell is one of its coauthors.
It lets a client put search criteria in the request body and send them safely and idempotently without changing server state—a good fit for AI search, where you ask but don't modify anything.

Adoption is underway: major browser vendors are discussing the RFC, and clients and frameworks such as curl and undici have already adopted it or are discussing adoption. Search for Agents supports plain text or JSON request bodies.
Starting today, Search for Agents is available to all customers, including the free plan—but the post only says "with limits."

Usage follows AI Search pricing: ingesting content, storing indexed content, and serving queries are all billed, and count toward your account's included usage and limits under the Workers Free and Paid plans.
In other words, free users can start using it, but the post doesn't state the free tier's specific quota.

list: The specific free tier limits—how many pages can be indexed or how many queries can be served per month—aren't given.
How often the index updates and how quickly new pages become searchable aren't specified; the post only says "see the developer docs."
No comparison of performance or pricing against similar ways to open website search to agents is provided.
No timeline is given for when QUERY will land in specific browsers or frameworks.
The specific rules for whether Search for Agents traffic from AI crawlers counts toward AI Crawl Control are not spelled out; the post only says it is "subject to your domain settings."

blocks.p: The value is saved effort: if you run a content or documentation site and want agents like OpenAI or OpenCode to be able to look up your material when they answer, you don't need to write code or maintain a search service, and the endpoint stays under your own domain.

The costs are also clear: your content will be crawled and indexed by Cloudflare, usage is billed under AI Search pricing, and the free tier has limits. What can actually be searched also depends on your WAF, bot management, and AI Crawl Control settings.

list: If you have a documentation or content site and want AI tools to be able to look up your pages, this toggle is the easiest place to start.
If you're already using Cloudflare and don't want to build your own retrieval backend, try it directly from Quick Actions.
If you're concerned about exposing content to agents, look at the Agent Readiness page and AI Crawl Control first, then decide whether to turn it on.
